content: This document does not address the off-label use of products or investigational products, except in cases where some recommendations may not align with package labeling. Approximately 45% of pregnancies in the United States are unintended, which is associated with increased risks of adverse maternal and infant health outcomes and higher healthcare costs. Women, men, and couples now have access to a growing number of safe and effective contraceptive methods, including long-acting reversible contraception such as intrauterine devices (IUDs) and implants, to reduce the risk of unintended pregnancies. However, with these expanded options comes the need for evidence-based guidance to assist healthcare providers in delivering high-quality family planning care. This includes selecting the most appropriate contraceptive method for individual circumstances and ensuring its correct, consistent, and continuous use to maximize effectiveness. In 2010, the CDC published the first U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (U.S. MEC), which provided recommendations on the safe use of contraceptive methods for women with various medical conditions and characteristics. This guidance was adapted from global recommendations developed by the World Health Organization (WHO). The U.S. MEC serves as a companion document to the U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use (U.S. SPR), which offers guidance on the safe and effective use of contraceptive methods once deemed medically appropriate. The WHO intended for its global guidance to be used by local or national policymakers, family planning program managers, and the scientific community as a reference when developing family planning guidance at the country or program level. Between 2008 and 2010, the CDC participated in a formal process to adapt the global guidance for use in the United States. This process included rigorous identification and critical appraisal of scientific evidence through systematic reviews and input from national experts on translating evidence into recommendations for U.S. healthcare providers. At that time, the CDC committed to keeping this guidance up to date and based on the best available evidence, with full reviews conducted every few years. This document updates the CDC's U.S. MEC 2010 based on new evidence and expert input. A summary of changes from the U.S. MEC 2010 is provided in Appendix A. Notable updates include the addition of recommendations for women with cystic fibrosis, multiple sclerosis, and those receiving certain psychotropic drugs or St. John's wort. Revisions were also made to recommendations for emergency contraception, including the addition of ulipristal acetate, and for postpartum women, breastfeeding women, and those with conditions such as dyslipidemias, migraine headaches, superficial venous disease, gestational trophoblastic disease, sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), and HIV. Recommendations for women receiving antiretroviral therapy were also updated. The goal of these recommendations is to remove unnecessary medical barriers to accessing and using contraception, thereby reducing the number of unintended pregnancies. These recommendations are intended to serve as clinical guidance for healthcare providers, who should always consider the individual clinical circumstances of each person seeking family planning services. This report is not a substitute for professional medical advice for individual patients, who should seek guidance from their healthcare providers when considering family planning options. Since the publication of the U.S. MEC 2010, the CDC has monitored the literature for new evidence relevant to the recommendations through the WHO/CDC Continuous Identification of Research Evidence (CIRE) system. This system identifies new evidence as it is published, allowing WHO and CDC to update systematic reviews and facilitate updates to recommendations as warranted by new evidence. Automated searches are conducted weekly in PubMed, and the results are reviewed. Abstracts meeting specific criteria are added to the web-based CIRE system, which facilitates coordination and peer review of systematic reviews for both WHO and CDC. In 2014, the CDC reviewed all existing recommendations in the U.S. MEC 2010 for new evidence identified by CIRE that could potentially lead to changes in recommendations. During August 27–28, 2014, the CDC held a meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, with 11 family planning experts and representatives from partner organizations to solicit input on the scope and process for updating both the U.S. MEC 2010 and U.S. SPR 2013. The participants included experts in family planning and represented various types of healthcare providers and organizations. A list of participants is provided at the end of this report. Meeting participants discussed topics to be addressed in the update of the U.S. MEC based on new evidence published since 2010, topics addressed at a 2014 WHO meeting to update global guidance, and suggestions received from healthcare providers for adding recommendations for women with medical conditions not yet included in the U.S. MEC. The CDC identified several topics for consideration when updating the guidance, including revisions to existing recommendations for certain medical conditions or characteristics (e.g., breastfeeding, postpartum, HIV, antiretroviral therapy, obesity, dyslipidemia, increased risk for STDs, superficial venous thrombosis, gestational trophoblastic disease, and migraine headaches), addition of recommendations for new medical conditions (e.g., cystic fibrosis, multiple sclerosis, use of certain psychotropic drugs, and St. John's wort), and addition of recommendations for new contraceptive methods (e.g., ulipristal acetate for emergency contraception). The CDC determined that all other recommendations in the U.S. MEC 2010 were up to date and consistent with the existing body of evidence for those recommendations. In preparation for a subsequent expert meeting held in August 2015 to review the scientific evidence for potential recommendations, CDC staff and other invited authors conducted independent systematic reviews for each of the topics being considered. The purpose of these systematic reviews was to identify direct evidence about the safety of contraceptive method use by women with selected conditions (e.g., risk for disease progression or other adverse health effects in women with multiple sclerosis who use combined hormonal contraceptives). Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines were followed for reporting systematic reviews, and the strength and quality of the evidence were assessed using the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force system. When direct evidence was limited or unavailable, indirect evidence (e.g., evidence on surrogate outcomes or among healthy women) and theoretical issues were considered and either added to direct evidence within a systematic review or separately compiled for presentation to the meeting participants. Completed systematic reviews were peer-reviewed by two or three experts and then provided to participants before the expert meeting. Reviews are referenced and cited throughout this document; the full reviews appear in the published literature and contain details of each review, including the systematic review question, literature search protocol, inclusion and exclusion criteria, evidence tables, and quality assessments. CDC staff continued to monitor new evidence identified through the CIRE system during the preparation for the August 2015 meeting. During August 26–28, 2015, in Atlanta, Georgia, the CDC held a meeting with 44 participants invited to provide their individual perspectives on the scientific evidence presented and potential recommendations. Twenty-nine of the participants represented a wide range of expertise in family planning provision and research, including obstetricians/gynecologists, pediatricians, family physicians, nurse practitioners, epidemiologists, and others with research and clinical practice expertise in contraceptive safety, effectiveness, and management. These individuals participated in the entire meeting. Fifteen participants with expertise relevant to specific topics on the meeting agenda provided information and participated in the discussion (e.g., an expert in cystic fibrosis was asked to provide general information about the condition and assist in interpreting the evidence and any theoretical concerns on the use of contraceptive methods in women with the condition). These participants provided input only during the session for which their topics were discussed. Lists of participants and any potential conflicts of interest are provided at the end of this report. During the meeting, the evidence from the systematic review for each topic was presented, including direct evidence and any indirect evidence or theoretical concerns. Participants provided their perspectives on using the evidence to develop recommendations that would meet the needs of U.S. healthcare providers. After the meeting, the CDC determined the recommendations in this report, taking into consideration the perspectives provided by the meeting participants. Feedback was also received from three external reviewers, composed of healthcare providers and researchers who had not participated in the update meetings. These reviewers were asked to provide comments on the accuracy, feasibility, and clarity of the recommendations. Areas of research that need additional investigation were also considered during the meeting. These recommendations are intended to help healthcare providers determine the safe use of contraceptive methods among women and men with various characteristics and medical conditions. Providers can also use the information in these recommendations when consulting with women, men, and couples about their selection of contraceptive methods. The tables in this document include recommendations for the use of contraceptive methods by women and men with particular characteristics or medical conditions. Each condition is defined as representing either an individual's characteristics (e.g., age or history of pregnancy) or a known preexisting medical or pathologic condition (e.g., diabetes or hypertension). The recommendations refer to contraceptive methods being used for contraceptive purposes; they do not consider the use of contraceptive methods for the treatment of medical conditions because the eligibility criteria in these situations might differ. The conditions affecting eligibility for the use of each contraceptive method are classified into one of four categories.
